chapter: Portraits from Hemphill to Getz, and the bebop question
title: Why bebop never moved him
summary: Horace admired Parker and Dizzy (whom he heard at Minton's) but could not play bebop and, on Fletcher's advice, stuck to swing and standards.

story.theme_name: Charlie Parker, Dizzy and the bebop revolution
story.community_name: Charlie Parker: encounters, lore and legacy

blocks.x: The reason I'm bringing that up is this one question I wanted to ask you, and we talked about this one time, but we didn't put it on tape -- is how did you feel about bebop when it was coming in and, you know, what

sort of relationship did you have to that? Did it influence you? Because I remember, for instance, Louis really put it down, and some of the older musicians who had been innovators in their time suddenly decided bebop was not music, and --

Tom, I hate to say this, but bebop never moved me. Number one is I couldn't play it, and I used to fool around and try to play some things. I learned in later years to play it a little, but I was told to stick more or less to the swing, you know? And while I admired Charlie Parker. I had nothing but the utmost musical respect for him, and also Dizzy Gillespie, because I know Dizzy played some gigs with me out of New York, and he where I found him, at Minton's place, Teddy Hill, used to play (inaudible) this is

-- and bebop was going there. A guy named Joe Guy, who was the first husband, I believe, of the late Billie Holiday, he played a gang of name with bebop. Another little old guy had a name named Benny, trumpet player, you (inaudible) know him.
We talked about him one time --
Man, he could play, And he played, that little runt, he could play bebop. ? I loved it. I had nothing against it, but I just -- I didn't dig it personally to play, and I didn't pattern

my band or my arrangements after that, just stuck with the old, hard swing, because I was told by my brother to always try and stick with the standards because they'd never die, and I intended to stay in this profession, I was going to have to rely upon the people with the money to support me, which I found out he was so right. I found out every day.
Oh, yeah. That's still true today.
